topicName: Non-SARGable Expressions and Functions on Columns
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding Non-SARGable Expressions and Functions in SQL Tuning"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"When tuning SQL queries, one of the most critical performance concepts to master is SARGability. The term stands for Search Argument Able. A query is considered SARGable if the database query optimizer can take advantage of an index to execute the query faster than by performing a full table scan."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"What Makes an Expression Non-SARGable?"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"An expression is non-SARGable when a function, mathematical operation, or explicit data type conversion is applied directly to a indexed column in the WHERE clause. When this happens, the database engine cannot traverse the B-tree index structure because the stored index values do not match the modified values in the predicate."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Applying scalar functions like UPPER(), LOWER(), SUBSTRING(), or YEAR() to a column."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Performing arithmetic operations such as column_name * 2 > 100."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Using implicit or explicit data type conversions where the column type differs from the search parameter type."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Bad Example: Non-SARGable Query"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Consider a table named 'Employees' with an index on the 'hire_date' column. The following query extracts employees hired in a specific year using a function on the column:"},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name
FROM Employees
WHERE YEAR(hire_date) = 2023;"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"Because the YEAR() function wraps the 'hire_date' column, the database engine must evaluate the function for every single row in the table, resulting in a costly full table scan."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Good Example: Rewriting as a SARGable Query"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"To fix this performance bottleneck, we must isolate the indexed column on one side of the comparison operator and move any functions or calculations to the parameter side."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name
FROM Employees
WHERE hire_date >= '2023-01-01'
  AND hire_date < '2024-01-01';"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"This rewritten query is fully SARGable. The database optimizer can now perform an index seek, rapidly locating the boundary pointers in the B-tree index for the year 2023."},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Database Developers"},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always keep columns bare in WHERE, JOIN, and HAVING clauses."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Be cautious of OR conditions combining SARGable and non-SARGable predicates, as the non-SARGable part may degrade the entire execution plan."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"If functions on columns are unavoidable due to business logic, consider creating a Computed Column persisted with an index, or implement a Functional Index (supported in engines like PostgreSQL and Oracle)."}]
